lessons.title: The reticulation pump station and its components
lessons.html:
What a reticulation pump station does

A reticulation pump station moves water from a source (reservoir, tank, dam or borehole) into a distribution network: pipes supplying irrigation zones, a farm village, livestock troughs or an estate. It must deliver the right flow at the right pressure, reliably, day after day.

Typical components

ComponentFunction
Sump or suction tankWater source for the pumps; level monitored
Suction manifold, strainers, isolating valvesFeed water to each pump; allow isolation
Duty and standby pumpsDuty pump runs normally; standby takes over on failure or maintenance; many stations alternate them to share wear
Non-return valvesPrevent backflow through stopped pumps
Delivery manifold, isolating valves, air valvesCombine pump outputs into the mainline
Pressure vessel or variable speed drive (VSD)Maintain pressure and reduce pump starts
Flow meter and pressure gauges or transmittersMeasure performance
Control panelStarters, protection relays, level and pressure controls, alarms, possibly telemetry
Surge protectionSurge vessels or valves to limit water hammer

Control methods

  • Pressure control: pressure switches or transmitters start and stop pumps between set points.
  • Level control: floats or level probes in the receiving reservoir start pumps when the level falls and stop them when full; low-level probes in the sump protect against dry running.
  • Variable speed drives: adjust pump speed to keep a constant pressure as demand changes, saving energy.
  • Timers: to pump in off-peak electricity periods where tariffs make this worthwhile.

Safety in the pump station

  • Only authorised, trained operators; electrical work by qualified electricians.
  • Lock out before mechanical work; keep guards on couplings.
  • Keep the station dry, lit and ventilated; water and electricity are a deadly combination.
  • Sumps and chambers can be confined spaces; never enter without a permit and standby person.
  • Hearing protection where noise is high.

lessons.title: Starting, running and stopping the station
lessons.html:
Before start-up

  1. Check the sump or source level is above the minimum.
  2. Check the suction and delivery isolating valves of the pump to be started are open as the procedure requires (some stations start against a partly closed delivery valve).
  3. Check the pump is primed: casing full of water, air bled.
  4. Check that guards are fitted, the area is clear, and no one is working on the system.
  5. Check the control panel: no alarms, selector switches in the correct mode (manual or auto), duty pump selected.

Starting

  • Start the pump from the panel. Watch the delivery pressure rise and the motor current settle (as indicated on the panel).
  • If starting against a partly closed valve, open it slowly to the normal position. Slow valve operation prevents water hammer.
  • Check for unusual noise, vibration, leaks and that the non-return valve operates.
  • Confirm flow on the flow meter.
  • Switch to automatic if that is the normal mode.

Monitoring during operation

ParameterWhy
Suction levelPrevent dry running and cavitation
Delivery pressureConfirms supply to network; sudden drop may mean a burst
FlowShows demand; unexpected high flow at night may indicate a leak
Motor current and temperatureOverload or bearing problems
Pump starts per hourToo many starts damages motors
Reservoir levelsConfirms the system is keeping up

Read and record values at set times on the log sheet or check telemetry.

Stopping

  1. For a manual stop, close the delivery valve slowly if the procedure requires, then stop the pump.
  2. For maintenance, isolate electrically and lock out, close suction and delivery valves, drain if needed.
  3. Make sure the standby pump is available so supply continues.

Power failures

After a power outage or load shedding, check the station restarts correctly, that no pump is running dry, and that time-based settings are still right. Stations with standby generators must have changeover switching installed by an electrician and generators tested regularly.

lessons.title: Responding to faults and keeping records
lessons.html:
Alarms and common faults

Alarm or symptomPossible causeFirst response
Low sump levelSource not refilling, borehole failing, valve closedConfirm pumps stopped; check supply; report
High pressureValve closed downstream, faulty controlStop pump if needed; find closed valve
Low pressure, high flowBurst pipeLocate burst; isolate section; report
Motor trip (overload)Mechanical binding, electrical fault, running off curveDo not keep resetting; call electrician; switch to standby
Pump runs but no flowLost prime, closed valve, broken couplingStop; check prime and valves
Frequent startingWaterlogged pressure tank, leaking non-return valve, small leakCheck tank charge and valves

Repeated resetting of an overload without finding the cause can burn out the motor. Report and escalate faults according to the station's procedure.

Routine maintenance by the operator

  • Keep the station clean and dry; remove rubbish and check drainage.
  • Check and clean suction strainers.
  • Exercise isolating valves periodically so they do not seize.
  • Alternate duty and standby pumps if not automatic.
  • Check gland drips, bearing temperatures, oil levels.
  • Report vibration, leaks and noise for maintenance.

Records

  • Log sheet: date, time, levels, pressures, flows, hours run, energy meter readings, pump in duty.
  • Incident and fault log: alarms, actions taken, who was notified.
  • Maintenance records: work done and parts used.
  • Water volumes: required where abstraction is licensed or registered under the National Water Act 36 of 1998.

Trends in flow and energy use help spot leaks and inefficient pumps, saving water and rand.

Key points

  • Know the station's components, control method and duty/standby arrangement.
  • Check levels, valves, prime and guards before start-up.
  • Open and close valves slowly to avoid water hammer.
  • Monitor level, pressure, flow, current and starts; record them.
  • Do not keep resetting tripped motors; find the cause and report.
